extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning discrete mathematics / introductory proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Worked solutions and methodological guidance for introductory discrete math exercises (logic, proofs, combinatorics, number theory). Shows how to construct truth tables, translate English to symbolic logic, negate quantified statements, and use standard proof techniques and counting principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use truth tables to determine logical truth and equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Write truth tables for compound formulas and compare the resulting columns: if the columns agree for all valuations then the statements are logically equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: several exercises show complete truth tables for formulas in P, Q, R and then conclude 'Thus since their columns agree, the two statements are logically equivalent.' Construct columns for each subformula (e.g., Q^R, P v (Q^R)) and the final formula, using all combinations of truth values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct truth tables by listing all truth-value combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: List all combinations of truth values for the atomic propositions and compute each subformula column to obtain the final truth column.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked tables enumerate rows for p, q, r (T/F combinations) and compute intermediate columns like Q^R, ~(P^Q), (P a ~P) v Q, etc.; ensure every subformula column is computed before the main connective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate English sentences into symbolic logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Map English sentences to propositional or predicate-symbolic form by identifying atomic propositions, quantifiers, and logical connectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: 'If f is a polynomial and its degree is greater than 2, then f is not constant' -> (P a Q) => R with definitions for P,Q,R; other translations show how to choose predicates and quantify appropriately (use explicit identifiers for predicates and quantifier structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negate quantified and compound statements correctly (swap quantifiers & negate predicates)
rubrics_metrics.description: To negate sentences with quantifiers, swap universal and existential quantifiers and negate the inner predicate; for compound statements apply DeMorgan's laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: negations of statements with 'for every' and 'there exists'; specific negations shown for epsilon-delta style statements and number-theoretic quantifications. Also shows negation of 'I don't eat anything that has a face' -> 'I will eat some things that have a face.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply DeMorgan's Laws for negation of logical connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ~(A v B) = ~A ^ ~B and ~(A ^ B) = ~A v ~B when negating compound formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly in negation exercises and when simplifying expressions like ~(P^Q) and in deriving that ~ (~ P v ~ Q) = P ^ Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove implications by direct proof using definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the antecedent and use definitions (e.g., even = 2k, odd = 2k+1, divisibility) to algebraically derive the consequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many examples: proving 'If x is even then x^2 is even' by writing x=2a and showing x^2=2(2a^2); proving divisibility statements by substituting definitions and factoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proof by contrapositive for implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove 'If P then Q' by proving the contrapositive 'If not Q then not P' when that is easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly used in many solutions (labelled '(Contrapositive)') e.g., to prove 'If n^2 is even then n is even' and similar parity/inequality implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proof by contradiction for existence and irrationality claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the negation of the claim (or that a counterexample exists), derive a logical contradiction, and conclude the original claim holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic examples include proofs that sqrt(2) and cube roots are irrational: assume rational representation in lowest terms, use divisibility/parity arguments to derive both numerator and denominator are even (contradiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by cases (case analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Break proofs into exhaustive cases (often parity or sign cases) and handle each separately to cover all possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used often: consider x even/odd, positive/negative, or x-y = 0 vs x-y ≠ 0 after factoring; each case yields the required conclusion. Page repeatedly structures proofs into 'Case 1', 'Case 2', etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use factoring to simplify expressions and deduce outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor algebraic expressions to reveal multiplicative structure that yields divisibility or equality conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: factoring x^2 - y^2 - 5x - 5y into (x - y)(x + y) - 5(x - y) to deduce (x - y)(x + y - 5), then use case analysis on x - y = 0 vs nonzero; factoring used widely to reduce to known patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the definition of divisibility and modular congruence directly
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate 'n divides (a-b)' into existence of integer k with a-b = nk and manipulate algebraically to prove congruence results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: proofs that congruence is preserved under polynomial operations (if a=b (mod n) then a^3 = b^3 (mod n)), or composing congruences by multiplying both sides and showing n divides difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express parity by 2k or 2k+1 and manipulate accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: When reasoning about even/odd, represent an integer as 2k (even) or 2k+1 (odd) and use algebra to show the parity of expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used extensively in parity proofs: showing sums/products/powers are even or odd by substitution; used in multiple examples (a^3 + a^2 + a, x^2 + 5x + 4, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove irrationality via lowest-terms rational representation and divisibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume sqrt(m) = a/b in lowest terms, square or cube both sides, deduce a and b share a prime factor (contradiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed for sqrt(2) and cube roots: show a and b must both be even (or divisible by 3) contradicting lowest-terms assumption; pattern is repeated across examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the Multiplication Principle for counting
rubrics_metrics.description: When forming lists/strings with independent choices for positions, multiply choice counts for each position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: number of length-4 lists from 6 letters = 6^4; binary strings length 8 = 2^8; used repeatedly in combinatorics exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting with constraints by dividing into types (case partitioning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Split the universe into mutually exclusive types that meet the constraint and sum counts per type, using the Multiplication Principle within each type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: counting 8-digit binary strings whose second or fourth digit is 1 by dividing into types (*1*****, *0*1****, *1*1****) and summing; counting lists containing two consecutive vowels by enumerating positions of the pair and counting per position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use complements and inclusion-exclusion for unions
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute sizes of unions via |A∪B| = |A| + |B| - |A∩B| and the general inclusion-exclusion formula for three sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: counting 4-digit numbers that are even or contain no 0's; computing |A∪B∪C| with inclusion-exclusion for strings that begin in 1, end in 1, or have exactly four 1's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use factorials and binomial coefficients for permutations and combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Model ordered lists as permutations and unordered selections as binomial coefficients; apply n!, nPk, and nCk appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 5-digit integers with no repeated digits and all digits odd -> 5!; number of 10-digit integers with exactly three 6's uses binomial choices for positions times choices for remaining digits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Binomial Theorem to obtain combinatorial identities and coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Extract coefficients or prove identities by expanding (x+y)^n and substituting specific values for x,y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: coefficient of x^8 in (x+2)^13 obtained by binomial coefficient times 2^5; proofs of sum identities like sum_{k=0}^n C(n,k) = 2^n and alternating sum equals 0 using (1+1)^n and (1-1)^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use paired-complement arguments to show parity or evenness of counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Pair each k-element subset with its complement to show counts are even (or to group into pairs), often used to prove binomial coefficients evenness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show C(2n,n) is even by pairing each n-element subset with its complement, giving an even total number of n-element subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue prime divisibility in factorial/binomial expressions via prime factorization
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prime p divides a factorial expression, analyze prime factors in the factorial decomposition to conclude divisibility of binomial coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to show if p is prime and 0

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'without loss of generality' to reduce symmetric cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statement is symmetric in certain variables, assume an ordering to simplify proof (e.g., assume a is even and b is odd).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in parity proofs: assume one variable has a specified parity to reduce the number of distinct cases while preserving generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare boolean/formula columns or rewrite implications using equivalences
rubrics_metrics.description: Use known logical equivalences (e.g., P=>Q = (~P) v Q) to rewrite and reason about formulas or to simplify truth-table work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises show rewriting P=>Q as (~P) v Q and use of identities like P ^ > Q = (~P) v Q in truth-table constructions and equivalence proofs.
